questions.q: If MPC = 0.8, the investment multiplier is:

questions.explanation: Haavelmo: equal rise in G and T raises Y by the same amount, so the multiplier is 1.

questions.q: The relative income hypothesis was given by:
questions.explanation: Duesenberry (1949): consumption depends on income relative to others and on past peak income (ratchet effect).

options: LM is horizontal; monetary policy is ineffective
LM is vertical; fiscal policy is ineffective
IS is vertical; monetary policy is effective
questions.explanation: At very low interest rates money demand is infinitely elastic, so extra money is just held; only fiscal policy works.

questions.q: Under perfect capital mobility and a fixed exchange rate (Mundell–Fleming), which policy is effective?
questions.explanation: Monetary expansion causes outflows that force the central bank to reverse it; fiscal expansion attracts inflows and is accommodated.

questions.q: Tobin's q is the ratio of:
options: Market value of firms to replacement cost of capital
questions.explanation: q > 1 means installing capital adds more value than it costs, so firms invest.

questions.q: The long-run Phillips curve according to Friedman and Phelps is:
options: Vertical at the natural rate of unemployment
questions.explanation: With adaptive expectations, any inflation rate is consistent with the natural rate in the long run.
Robert Barro (1974): debt-financed tax cuts do not raise consumption because people save for future taxes.
Kitchin: short inventory cycles of about 40 months.

questions.q: National income (NNP at factor cost) equals:
options: NNP at market prices − net indirect taxes
questions.explanation: NNP at FC = NNP at MP − (indirect taxes − subsidies).

questions.q: The policy ineffectiveness proposition is associated with:
questions.explanation: With rational expectations and flexible prices, anticipated monetary policy does not affect real output.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason for a downward-sloping AD curve?
questions.explanation: The ratchet effect belongs to Duesenberry's consumption theory, not to AD.

questions.q: The paradox of thrift implies that an increase in the saving propensity may:
options: Reduce income without raising total saving
questions.explanation: Higher saving lowers demand and income; total saving may not rise (it can even fall if investment is induced).
About 2–3% of output is lost for each 1 percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate.

questions.q: The permanent income hypothesis predicts that a one-time lottery win will be:
questions.explanation: Transitory income has a very low MPC; it is mostly saved and spread over time.
